s04.slug: FRIDAY · 1:15 PM · I-10 EAST, BLYTHE → THE COLORADO RIVER
body: Jack wakes at Blythe with his face against the window and the sun full on it, the windmills two and a half hours gone. Out in the desert, for no reason the last hundred miles have offered, there are fields: alfalfa as green as a pool table, irrigation ditches running full and ruler-straight beside it, a stand of date palms around a farmhouse with a pickup parked under them and both its doors open.
The RAZR in his lap has two from Burnaby.

A weather report, and a minute behind it a forecast. Eight degrees is about forty-six. It’s raining on her in Canada, and by her own rules she’s already missing him tomorrow. He doesn’t answer yet. He’d like to have some weather of his own first.

The Colorado comes up under the van green, which nobody told him, with reeds along both banks and a row of aluminum boats nosed in under an RV park, the river that cut the Grand Canyon looking like it has never heard of the place. A sign at the end of the bridge welcomes them to Arizona.
“It’s two-twenty in Arizona,” Kevin says. “We lost an hour. I’m logging it.” He holds his thumbnail on the hour button of the dash clock until the clock agrees with the state.

Ehrenberg is the first exit, and Kevin takes it. He tops off, because “Arizona’s thirty cents cheaper. That’s not a preference,” and has the hood up before the pump clicks. He pulls the dipstick, wipes it on a blue shop towel, pushes it home, pulls it again and holds it up to the sun. Frank Costigan loses to a pre-med again, in a second state.

The receipt comes back to the van with Kevin. He hands it in to Margot, and Margot reaches it back over her headrest into the way-back, where a pen writes it down on a legal pad. It travels the left side of the van and never comes near Jack’s, which is the system, and the system works.
He texts his father.

body.text: kevin checked the oil at the az line

body: Then he has weather.
A report, not a forecast. Out here he isn’t sending her anything from the future.

Theo takes the keys at the pump. Kevin gets in on the passenger side and leans across to fix Theo’s mirrors, both of them, while Theo looks for the ignition on the wrong side of the wheel. Margot stays where she is, beside Jack, with La Paz County printed out on her knees in yellow highlighter.
Past the truck scales the RAZR buzzes against his leg.
Jack shuts the phone and puts it in his shirt pocket, flat, where he’ll feel the next one come in.
“Sixty-four,” Kevin says. “Sixty-five. Hold it there.” Ahead the desert opens out flat to a line of bare brown mountains, and the needle holds. “That’s beautiful, Theo.”

s05.slug: FRIDAY · 5:05 PM · I-10 EAST, PHOENIX → THE GILA RIVER — EIGHT
body: Kevin has turned the mix off. He did it at the Phoenix city limits, ejected the disc into its sleeve and said, “Atmosphere,” and since then the Odyssey has had the tires, the fan in the dash and Kevin.

Theo has it through downtown and into the Broadway Curve at Friday rush hour, eight lanes of Phoenix going home with the low sun behind them flashing off every rear window ahead, and Kevin talks him across it like a delivery. “You’ve got a gap. You’ve got a gap. Breathe. Signal. Okay — *now*.” The Odyssey goes in between a cement truck and a Camry. Kevin sits back. “And we’re in. Everybody’s healthy.”
“I was born at Cedars-Sinai,” Theo says, “with less coaching.”
In Chandler, Margot’s Nokia buzzes in the milk crate at her feet. She reads it, puts it back, and says to the van at large, without malice, “Eight now.”
Nobody asks eight what. Margot tells them anyway, in ascending order of reliability, with Maricopa County open on her knees.

“The one where the dog gives an interview. That’s Doug’s. Kenzie Rourke’s, in which somebody threw a glass. The Forum table’s, in which Caleb says Hale chaired it like a Lambeth Conference. The Classics department’s, which still has a chorus and is now about Thucydides. Priya’s, which has a form number. Joey Abruzzo’s, which I’ve only heard from two floors away.” She turns a page of Arizona. “Becca’s is a refusal to have one. She said she wasn’t there and she isn’t going to be. I’m counting it.”
She lets a semi go by on the left. “And the eighth, by Nokia, just now. Julian heard about it and said nothing.” She looks out at Chandler. “That one’s my favorite. It’s the only accurate one.”
From the way-back, directly behind Jack, Laney says, “Margot. *Hush*, or I’m telling them version nine.”
“There isn’t a version nine.”
“Not yet there isn’t.”
Margot addresses the back of Kevin’s headrest. “Kevin hasn’t contributed one.”
“I don’t have the information,” Kevin says, with his eyes on Theo’s speedometer.

After that the Odyssey is miserable in four directions. Theo tries a pitch on a billboard past the last of the subdivisions, a personal-injury lawyer forty feet wide with his arms folded — “Open on a mustache. A man in Mesa has been wronged, and he has a *feeling* about it —” and lets it go, and drives. Laney opens a bag of Twizzlers and says, “Isn’t this nice. Isn’t this just the nicest,” and eats them one after another behind her sunglasses. Kevin tells everybody what a great car this is, and at the next exit what great mileage it gets, and at the one after that he stops. Margot reads the counties.

Jack was at the original. So were Theo and Laney, up front and right behind him, and not one of the three of them corrects a word of any of the eight. The Gila River goes under them a few miles on, a quarter mile of sand and tamarisk with a river somewhere in it and a sign to say so.

From the way-back, left side, nothing. He and Lena say nothing at all, across the reservation and the long flat after it, while the sun comes around into the right-hand windows and lies across Margot’s maps.

Past Casa Grande a green sign comes up for the Picacho Peak exit, and beyond it the peak itself stands up out of the flat, one black broken tooth against the west, with the last of the sun burning along its edges.
